ethiopia.title: Red Cross Warns of Worsening Humanitarian Crisis in Oromia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Red Cross Cautions of Worsening Humanitarian Crisis in Oromia As Conflict, Displacement Deepen Civilian Hardship - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Red Cross Cautions of Worsening Humanitarian Crisis in Oromia As Conflict, Displacement Deepen Civilian Hardship Addis Standard Internally displaced people from the Oromo community in western Oromia shelter in Adama, Ganda Saqaqalloo area, receive community support at a mosque (file photo) 19 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has warned that the humanitarian situation in Ethiopia's Oromia region is deteriorating amid persistent armed conflict, deadly civilian attacks and growing displacement, saying it is struggling to reach all communities affected by the escalating insecurity. The organization said on Thursday that communities across several zones of Oromia were enduring severe hardship as fighting and insecurity continued to disrupt their lives. The ICRC, working alongside the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS), said it had intensified humanitarian assistance in conflict-affected areas, particularly in western and southern Oromia, over recent weeks. Oromia has been grappling with a protracted armed conflict involving federal forces and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) since 2019, alongside increasingly fragmented security crises, intercommunal violence and clashes along regional boundaries. The deteriorating security situation has also been accompanied by growing public grievances over local governance, alleged coercive practices and economic disruption. Lat October and early November saw a spike in civilian causalities after armed men killed at least 48 people were killed and more than 31 others seriously injured in a six-hour assault on in Shirka Woreda in Southeast Oromia zone. A subsequent attack in the area reportedly claimed dozens more lives. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The latest security crisis has also intensified along the Oromia-Somali regional border . Fighting erupted in Moyale on October 18 following a dispute over the display of a regional flag and the fatal shooting of a 13-year-old girl, subsequently spreading across several districts along the border between the two regions. The clashes have triggered significant displacement, disrupted local services and deepened food insecurity. The fighting has also paralyzed livestock markets and cross-border trade , further undermining pastoralist livelihoods in Borana. Meanwhile, insecurity persists in parts of Wollega, in western Oromia zone, where conflict involving overlapping armed factions continues to expose civilians to risks of displacement and restricted access to essential services. Igor Moroz, deputy head of the Red Cross Oromia Regional Office, said the organization was conducting relief operations in conflict-affected areas, including the former East Wollega, Horo Guduru Wollega, Guji and Borana zones. "Our team is doing everything they can to reach those suffering amidst the conflict and war with aid," Moroz said. The organization said it had assisted tens of thousands of households in recent weeks through its local branches. Its interventions included providing medical assistance to 125,000 patients, rehabilitating and handing over two health centers to local communities, and undertaking work on two additional facilities. In response to water shortages, the Red Cross said it had constructed 300 hand-pump water points, benefiting more than 90,000 people. It also distributed agricultural tools to over 7,000 households to help communities affected by the crisis restore their livelihoods. Additionally, the organization said it had provided financial assistance to 2,900 households that lost property due to conflict in the former East Wollega, West Wollega and East Borana zones. The statement also highlighted the plight of 2,300 displaced households in Sasiga and Angar, which faced severe hardship at the beginning of the year. A Red Cross official said an assessment visit found displaced residents in distress and without basic possessions, prompting the organization to provide water and other essential services. As insecurity persists, the Red Cross said it had engaged armed actors, government authorities and religious leaders to stress the importance of respecting international humanitarian law. It had also trained first responders in the proper handling of human remains during emergency situations. It is also closely monitoring humanitarian emergencies linked to insecurity across Ethiopia. According to a social media post by the Prime Minister, the project covers the Bole Medhanialem-Golagul-British Embassy, Bole Medhanialem-Moenco, Bole School-Adey Abeba Model Village, and Imperial Hotel-Shalla Park corridors. The project also includes the Chechnya-Bole Rwanda and Adey Abeba Stadium-Bole Road routes, alongside connecting internal roads. The Prime Minister said the initiative is part of the Medemer Government's broader urbanization strategy, which seeks to transform cities into productive centers of enterprise, trade, knowledge, culture, institutional development and employment. It also incorporates the renovation of schools, libraries, playgrounds and sports fields, as well as the development of cafés, restaurants and green public plazas, with an emphasis on improving public amenities and residents' quality of life. PM Abiy underscored that the quality of urban development increasingly shapes a country's productivity, human dignity, social order and environmental resilience. He added that the project is part of a broader vision to build productive, inclusive, green and resilient cities capable of accommodating future population growth while responding to climate challenges and evolving infrastructure needs. The UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it strongly rejected what it described as unwarranted treatment by the Somali government, characterizing the actions as damaging to bilateral relations and cooperation between the two countries. UAE Cites “Hostile” Steps as Basis for Withdrawal The Emirati statement said that decisions affecting relations between the two governments should be based on shared interests and should avoid political considerations and internal Somali disputes. The UAE also stated that it has never been a party to Somalia’s internal conflicts related to power struggles, noting that such matters can negatively affect the interests of both peoples. According to the statement, the decision to close the embassy and recall diplomats in January 2026 came after steps the UAE described as hostile, including the termination of bilateral agreements. This refers to the Somali Cabinet’s January decision to annul all agreements with the UAE, including port and security cooperation pacts, which was reported by FTL Somalia at the time. The UAE said it holds great appreciation for the Somali people, particularly Somali communities residing in the Emirates, businesspeople, and others with ties to both nations. It pledged to preserve the historical relationship and shared interests between the peoples of Somalia and the UAE. Background to the Rupture The formal response follows a series of escalations. This week, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud delivered a televised address accusing the UAE of interference, including signing port deals outside federal authority and establishing parallel security structures, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage . UAE Presidential Adviser Anwar Gargash responded days later, describing the speech as an “attack” but not addressing the specific allegations, as reported here . Somalia subsequently expelled the UAE ambassador and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, a move FTL Somalia reported . The UAE’s latest statement confirms that its diplomatic presence had already been terminated months earlier. The dispute has also intersected with UAE engagement in Somaliland, where Dubai-based DP World has invested heavily in Berbera Port. The UAE hosted Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro in Dubai in May with elevated protocol, as reported by FTL Somalia . FTL Critical Note The UAE’s formal response is notable for what it does not say. It does not address the specific allegations Mohamud raised: the port deals signed with regional administrations, the military bases outside federal command, the Berbera incident involving a Yemeni militia leader, or the UAE’s alleged role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. Instead, it frames the dispute as a matter of Somali internal politics and “hostile” Somali actions. That framing serves Abu Dhabi’s interests, but it leaves the core disputes unresolved. The Somali government’s case has its own vulnerabilities, it accuses a foreign power of undermining sovereignty while it cannot control the regional administrations that signed the deals or prevent external actors from cultivating relationships with those regions. Neither side has articulated what it would concede to restore a functional relationship. Until one does, the diplomatic rupture remains a stalemate conducted through statements rather than negotiations. somalia.content: Somalia expels UAE ambassador, gives him 72 hours to leave country - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia expels UAE ambassador, gives him 72 hours to leave country Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Thursday November 19, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali federal government on Thursday ordered the United Arab Emirates' ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours and recalled its ambassador from Abu Dhabi for consultations. The decisions were announced following a weekly Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre in Mogadishu, where ministers reviewed a Foreign Ministry report outlining what the government described as threats to Somalia's sovereignty, independence and national security. advertisements Information Minister Abdulfatah Qasim Mohamud announced the measures at a news conference, saying the Cabinet had directed the Foreign Ministry to notify the Emirati ambassador of the order to leave Somalia. The ministry was also instructed to summon Somalia's ambassador to the UAE for consultations with the federal government. The Cabinet further directed the Foreign Ministry to inform the international community about what Mogadishu described as continued interference by Abu Dhabi in Somalia's domestic affairs. The government said it would pursue lawful measures to counter actions it considers violations of the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The information minister also warned individuals and groups against cooperating in activities that the government alleges are intended to undermine Somalia's independence and national unity. Thursday's decision follows a sharp escalation in diplomatic tensions between Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi over the past several days. In a televised address Tuesday, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the UAE of providing financial, political and security assistance to armed groups and regional administrations opposed to the federal government. He also accused Abu Dhabi of establishing military facilities and supporting security arrangements outside the control of Somalia's national institutions. Hassan Sheikh criticized agreements between the UAE and the administrations of Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland involving the strategic ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo, arguing that such arrangements should be negotiated through the federal government. "The Council instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation to recall Somalia's ambassador to the UAE... and to notify the UAE ambassador to Somalia to leave the country within 72 hours," Somalia's Information Minister Abdulfatah Qasim said. The expulsion followed a cabinet meeting at which the UAE was accused of "blatant aggression against Somalia". "The Somali government is taking a series of measures... to defend the country against UAE actions targeting its sovereignty, territorial integrity, national unity, internal security and independence," Qasim said. The UAE foreign ministry condemned the move. In a statement, it said it "strongly denounced the escalatory and hostile approach by the Somali government toward the UAE". The expulsion reflected "irresponsible positions that undermine bilateral relations and weaken the foundations of cooperation between the two countries", it added. - Regional disputes - On Tuesday, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud criticised the UAE in a state of the nation address, accusing it of fuelling "political discord" in the Horn of Africa country. "The UAE has provided political and financial support to certain regional states, enabling them to oppose the federal government," Mohamud said. "It has encouraged political discord and fuelled division among Somalis to undermine the authority of the state and make the country easier to control from outside," he added. Mohamud has been facing hostility from leaders in several of Somalia's federal states, including the powerful territories of Puntland and Jubaland, who complain of the central government encroaching on their powers. Federal forces have also removed the governor of South West state, leading to fierce fighting. In January, Somalia cancelled all agreements with the UAE after Israel's recognition of Somaliland. The cancellation also came after the UAE allegedly helped a Yemeni separatist leader escape by boat and plane through Somali ports without consulting the government. - Contested ports - Somalia lies at a strategic point, on a major trade route between the Indian Ocean and the Suez Canal. The UAE built and operates a large deep-water port and military base at Berbera in Somaliland and two others at Bosaso and Kismayo in other parts of Somalia. Although the Somali government said the UAE would no longer be permitted to operate the ports, Somalia is deeply fragmented and the federal government has practically no control over the semi-autonomous states where the ports are located. The UAE statement voiced "regret over the Somali government's attempts to bring its internal power struggles into bilateral relations". Mohamud accused the UAE of intervening in Libya and Yemen and of also seeking to divide Somalia and Sudan. In Sudan, the UAE is widely accused of arming the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitaries, who have been fighting the regular military since 2023 and are accused of massacres against civilians. The government called on the UAE to conduct its relations with Somalia exclusively through federal institutions, citing the United Nations Charter and international law. The statement follows a televised address Tuesday by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who accused the UAE of providing political, financial and security support to regional administrations and armed groups that he said were undermining Somalia's unity. Hassan Sheikh also criticized agreements involving the UAE and the administrations of Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland, particularly arrangements concerning the strategic ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo. He argued that such agreements must be negotiated through the federal government because the ports are national assets belonging to the Somali people. The president further accused Abu Dhabi of establishing military and security structures outside federal control, allegations that have not been independently verified. Somalia's latest diplomatic statement comes amid an escalating public exchange between officials in Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi. Earlier Wednesday, Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, criticized Hassan Sheikh's remarks, accusing him of prioritizing personal political interests over Somalia's national interests. Gargash defended the UAE's longstanding relationship with Somalia and warned that domestic political rivalries should not draw the country into wider regional disputes. The government warned that it would pursue lawful measures to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity. “The Federal Republic of Somalia will take all necessary lawful measures to safeguard its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national unity,” the statement concluded. The ministry did not specify what additional measures it intended to take or whether further diplomatic restrictions against the UAE were being considered. The latest confrontation follows Somalia's January decision to terminate agreements with the UAE covering security, defense and economic cooperation, including arrangements involving regional ports. The dispute has intensified amid political disagreements between Mogadishu and several regional administrations over constitutional amendments, power-sharing and the country's electoral process. The UAE maintains economic and security relationships with Somaliland and other Somali regional authorities, while Mogadishu insists that foreign governments must respect the federal government's authority over international relations. REUTERS/Rula Rouhana SHARE Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Abu Dhabi (Somalia Today) — The United Arab Emirates on Thursday denounced what it called the Somali government’s “escalatory and hostile approach”, hours after Mogadishu ordered the Emirati ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours. In a statement, the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Mogadishu’s stance reflected “irresponsible positions that undermine bilateral relations and weaken the foundations of cooperation between the two countries”. Abu Dhabi did not directly address the expulsion deadline for its envoy, Ahmed Jumaa Alremeithi. Instead, the ministry stated that the UAE had already closed its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawn its diplomatic staff in January 2026. In a statement on 4 May , Somalia’s foreign ministry had dismissed earlier reports that the envoy had been expelled and said the mission was operating as usual. Somalia Today can also confirm that Alremeithi was still working in Mogadishu at the time of Thursday’s order, though the UAE had scaled back its embassy staff months earlier. Somalia’s cabinet earlier on Thursday gave Alremeithi 72 hours to leave and recalled its own ambassador from Abu Dhabi for consultations, accusing the Gulf state of “blatant aggression”. Information Minister Abdulfatah Kasim Mohamud warned that Mogadishu would take action against anyone cooperating with the UAE in what he termed an “invasion” of Somalia. Defence Minister Ahmed Moalim Fiqi wrote on X telling the envoy to “pack your bags and leave”. Internal power struggles In its response, the Emirati foreign ministry urged that diplomatic decisions be guided by shared interests and kept “free of political considerations and internal conflicts”. The ministry expressed regret over what it described as the Somali government’s attempts “to bring its internal power struggles into bilateral relations in a manner which could adversely affect the interests of the two brotherly peoples”. That language echoed remarks made a day earlier by Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, who questioned whether Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was putting his personal interests ahead of Somalia’s. Gargash referred to Mohamud as the “outgoing Somali president” and blamed domestic political rivalries for drawing Somalia into regional disputes. Mogadishu is embroiled in a constitutional standoff after Somalia’s attorney general rejected a Supreme Court ruling this month declaring that Mohamud’s presidential mandate had expired. Despite its sharp criticism of federal officials, the UAE foreign ministry sought to separate the government in Mogadishu from the wider population. It affirmed its “deep appreciation for the brotherly Somali people” and highlighted ties with the Somali community living in the UAE and Somali visitors. “The UAE remains committed to preserving and strengthening these ties and shared interests,” the ministry said. ‘Embassy closure’ The ministry said its January 2026 embassy closure and staff withdrawal followed “hostile practices by the Somali government toward the UAE’s embassy and policies”, including Mogadishu’s move to scrap bilateral accords. On 12 January, Somalia’s federal cabinet announced it was cancelling all agreements with the UAE, covering ports, government institutions, defence and security, citing violations of national sovereignty. Regional administrations in Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland rejected Mogadishu’s authority to terminate their arrangements with Abu Dhabi, leaving commercial and security ties on the ground largely intact. Puntland said its agreement with a subsidiary of Dubai-based DP World to operate Bosaso port remained in force. DP World also continues to operate the strategic port of Berbera on the Gulf of Aden under a concession signed with Somaliland. Meanwhile, Senior Somali sources told Reuters on Thursday that the UAE had continued paying salaries and providing logistical backing for roughly 3,400 Somali military police and special forces troops in and around Mogadishu. Ports and regional disputes Tensions flared anew this week after President Mohamud delivered a televised address on Tuesday accusing Abu Dhabi of bypassing the federal government to strike deals over the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo. Mohamud alleged that the Emirates had established unauthorised military bases, armed forces outside the national chain of command and backed regional administrations opposed to Mogadishu while federal troops battle Al-Shabaab militants. He also accused the UAE of helping facilitate Israel’s recognition of Somaliland last December and using Berbera in January to transfer Yemeni separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi without federal consent. The UAE and the African Union Commission had reaffirmed support for Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity in a joint statement on 6 January. Somaliland’s foreign ministry dismissed Mogadishu’s claims on Thursday, asserting exclusive authority over its territory and foreign agreements. “Somaliland exercises exclusive authority over its territory and foreign relations,” its foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday, adding that Hargeisa could enter into diplomatic, economic and strategic agreements without Mogadishu’s approval. (IHA Photo) Mogadishu (HOL) — Turkish F-16 fighter jets deployed in Somalia have completed a long-range rotation between Mogadishu and Türkiye, covering more than 11,000 kilometers in two flights without intermediate landings, Türkiye's Ministry of National Defence announced Tuesday. The ministry said the aircraft traveled a combined 11,038 kilometers (6,859 miles), equivalent to 5,960 nautical miles, between Mogadishu and Bandırma in northwestern Türkiye's Balıkesir province. advertisements The operation, completed over 55 hours, was carried out by pilots from the 161st Squadron of Türkiye's 6th Main Jet Base Command as part of scheduled maintenance rotations for aircraft serving under the Somali-Turkish Task Force Air Component Command. According to the ministry, the flights were conducted without intermediate landings, demonstrating the Turkish Air Force's ability to carry out long-distance military deployments. The ministry described the operation as an exceptional achievement for fighter aircraft and said it highlighted Türkiye's strategic force projection capabilities and continued commitment to security and stability in East Africa. The two sorties covered an average distance of more than 5,500 kilometers each. Such long-distance operations require aerial refueling support for F-16 fighter jets flying without intermediate landings. However, the ministry did not disclose the number of aircraft involved or provide details about the refueling arrangements used during the mission. Türkiye deployed three F-16 fighter jets to Somalia on Jan. 28, 2026, expanding its military presence in the Horn of Africa country. The aircraft were stationed at Aden Adde International Airport in Mogadishu, where hangars had been constructed ahead of their arrival. Their deployment marked a further expansion of military cooperation between Türkiye and Somalia, which have developed close defense and security relations over the past decade. Türkiye operates a major military training facility in Mogadishu, known as TURKSOM, where Turkish instructors have trained thousands of Somali military personnel. More than 5,000 Somali security personnel have reportedly received training through Turkish military programs, while additional Somali troops have undergone specialized training in Türkiye. The two countries also signed a defense and maritime cooperation agreement in 2024 aimed at strengthening Somalia's maritime security and military capabilities. Türkiye has continued providing military training, equipment and advisory support to Somalia as the country conducts operations against al-Shabab, the al-Qaeda-linked militant group. The latest aircraft rotation comes as Somalia seeks to strengthen its security forces and assume greater responsibility for national security amid changes to the African Union peacekeeping mission. The Turkish Defence Ministry did not indicate whether the aircraft involved in the maintenance rotation had been replaced or when they would return to Somalia. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Somalia: Djibouti peacekeepers killed in clash with Hawadle militias at Beledweyne airport Somalia: Djibouti peacekeepers killed in clash with Hawadle militias at Beledweyne airport November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Two Djiboutian peacekeepers were killed and two others wounded on Thursday when African Union troops clashed with Hawadle clan militias who seized Beledweyne’s Ugaas Khalif Airport to block a plane carrying federal government troops from landing, local reports and a militia spokesman said. The brief fighting broke out after Macawisley fighters moved onto the runway and surrounding areas of the airstrip on the edge of the central Somali town. Djiboutian forces based nearby attempted to push them back and clear the way for the aircraft. The plane aborted its landing and returned to its point of departure. At least five Macawisley fighters were injured in the exchange. “We will never again allow a plane carrying federal troops to land at the airstrip,” Mumin Mohamed Halane, who identified himself as a spokesman for the Macawisley, told The Somali Stream. The clash marks a sharp escalation of weeks of tensions in Beledweyne, the capital of the Hiran region in Somalia’s Hirshabelle state. Hawadle militias have been mobilizing in large numbers alongside hundreds of soldiers and security personnel who left their positions in the national army and other security agencies after clan leader Ugaas Yusuf Ugas Hassan called on them to report to his residence. He framed the mobilization as a defense of the town against what he described as an impending offensive by rival clans acting in the name of the federal government. On Sunday, tens of thousands of protesters filled the streets of Beledweyne opposing both the federal government in Mogadishu and the Hirshabelle administration. Federal efforts to ease the standoff have so far failed to persuade clan leaders. Beledweyne has long been a flashpoint for clan rivalries and security operations. The Macawisley, drawn mainly from the Hawadle clan, previously fought alongside government forces against Al-Shabaab but have grown increasingly hostile to federal and regional authorities amid disputes over leadership and power-sharing. Control of the airport – and the ability to move troops by air – has become a central point of contention as both sides dig in. The situation remains fluid, with the risk of further confrontation if the standoff continues. 14 عاماً من الصراع، لا تزال كرة القدم النسائية تواجه تحديات كبيرة، بعدما تسببت الحرب في تعطيل المسابقات وتشتت اللاعبات بين دول مختلفة، إلى جانب توقف النشاط الدولي لسنوات. وقالت نور جمعة، حارسة مرمى المنتخب السوري السابقة، إن جيلها «احترق وضاع بالكامل»، مضيفة أن كل ما كان يجري بناؤه اختفى فجأة. وكان المنتخب السوري للسيدات قد خاض أول مباراة دولية له عام 2005، وبدأت في 2011 خطط لإطلاق دوري نسائي لكرة القدم بنظام 11 لاعبة، لكن اندلاع الاحتجاجات والحرب أدى إلى التخلي عن تلك المشاريع. وعلى مدى السنوات الست التالية، توقفت كرة القدم النسائية في البلاد عملياً، واقتصر النشاط على بعض بطولات كرة الصالات، بينما غادر أكثر من ستة ملايين شخص سوريا، بينهم مئات المرتبطين بالرياضة. وفي حين استمر نشاط منتخب الرجال، الذي خاض مبارياته الدولية خارج البلاد بعد منع سوريا من استضافة اللقاءات عام 2011 لأسباب أمنية، غابت المساحات التي يمكن للفتيات من خلالها ممارسة اللعبة أو متابعة منتخب وطني نسائي يمثل بلادهن. وبحسب صحيفة «الغارديان» البريطانية، تروي رنيم أبو لطيف، حارسة مرمى المنتخب السوري البالغة 21 عاماً، كيف بدأت علاقتها بكرة القدم بعدما كانت تشاهد مباريات منتخب الرجال وتتمنى وجود منتخب للفتيات. وجاءتها الفرصة مصادفة عندما أخبرتها فتاة تسكن بجوار منزل عائلتها بوجود نادٍ للفتيات، لتصف التجربة بأنها كانت أشبه بتحقق الأحلام. أما جلنار مصطفى، المولودة عام 2008، فكانت تمضي ساعات في اللعب مع الفتيان في حيها بمدينة الحسكة، قبل أن تلفت مقاطع فيديو نشرتها عبر «فيسبوك» انتباه أحد المدربين، الذي دعاها للانضمام إلى فريقه. لكنها أشارت إلى أن ممارسة الرياضة لا تزال تواجه قيوداً اجتماعية، خصوصاً في شمال البلاد، حيث قالت إن الرياضة «ممنوعة تماماً على الفتيات». وحاول المنتخب السوري العودة إلى المنافسات الدولية في أبريل (نيسان) 2017، عندما شارك في تصفيات كأس آسيا بفيتنام، بعد ست سنوات من التوقف. وجاء الاستعداد للبطولة محدوداً، إذ جُمعت اللاعبات عبر اختبارات أُعلن عنها على «فيسبوك»، ولم يحصل الفريق سوى على نحو شهر من التحضير. وخسر المنتخب جميع مبارياته، بينها هزيمة ثقيلة أمام ميانمار بنتيجة 14-صفر. وتعرضت اللاعبات لانتقادات واسعة رغم ضعف الإعداد، وهو ما دفع مها الكتريب، التي شاركت في تلك البطولة، إلى التوجه نحو التدريب والعمل الإداري، بهدف بناء قاعدة قادرة على إعداد جيل جديد. وأسهمت لاحقاً في تأسيس برنامج لتطوير كرة القدم النسائية، كما أعدت أول استراتيجية سورية للعبة، قُدمت إلى الاتحاد الدولي لكرة القدم «فيفا»، بهدف زيادة المشاركة النسائية ووضع مسار واضح للوصول إلى المنتخبات الوطنية. وشهد عام 2019 تأسيس دوري نسائي للكبار بمشاركة ستة فرق، قبل إطلاق منتخبات للفئات العمرية، بينما أقيمت هذا العام النسخة الأولى من دوري الناشئات. واستهدفت الاستراتيجية التي أعدتها الكتريب زيادة مشاركة النساء في كرة القدم بنسبة 150 في المائة خلال أربع سنوات، من خلال إنشاء 33 مركزاً تدريبياً في المدارس موزعة على 11 محافظة، بطاقة استيعابية تصل إلى 1650 فتاة بحلول عام 2026. لكن الأرقام تكشف حجم الفجوة التي لا تزال قائمة؛ ففي عام 2022 لم يتجاوز عدد اللاعبات المسجلات ألف لاعبة من أصل 25 ألف لاعب ولاعبة في سوريا. وعلى صعيد البنية التحتية، أعلنت وزارة الرياضة والشباب إعادة تأهيل 48 منشأة رياضية خلال عام 2025، مع خطط لإصلاح نحو 150 منشأة إضافية وبناء قرابة 20 منشأة جديدة بحلول 2028، في إطار مساعٍ لاستعادة القدرة على استضافة المنافسات وفق متطلبات «فيفا» والاتحاد الآسيوي لكرة القدم. ورغم هذه الخطوات، لا تزال الانتقادات تطال أداء الاتحاد السوري لكرة القدم وسرعة تطوير اللعبة، خصوصاً من جانب أيزوك، البالغة 26 عاماً، بوصفها إحدى أبرز اللاعبات السوريات اللواتي خضن تجربة الاحتراف خارج البلاد. ففي عام 2023 أصبحت أول لاعبة سورية مولودة في البلاد توقع عقداً احترافياً، عندما انضمت إلى نادي نجمة جدة السعودي، بعد أن لفتت الأنظار بأدائها في المنافسات المحلية. لكن انتقالها لم يكن سهلاً، إذ تسببت مشكلات التأشيرة والأوراق الرسمية في تأخر وصولها حتى قبل يومين فقط من انطلاق الموسم، ولم تستمر تجربتها سوى بضعة أشهر قبل أن تعود إلى سوريا، ثم تنتقل لاحقاً للعب في الأردن. وقالت أيزوك إن الفارق بين ظروف كرة القدم في سوريا وخارجها كبير، سواء من حيث المعاملة أو التدريبات أو المنشآت، مشيرة إلى أن اللاعبات في سوريا يواجهن ضغوطاً نفسية وصعوبات كبيرة من أجل تحقيق أبسط النجاحات. وأضافت أن تجربتها خارج البلاد تمثل رسالة أمل، لإثبات أن اللاعبات قادرات على النجاح رغم الظروف الصعبة والحرب. وتظل الأزمة المالية إحدى أكبر العقبات أمام تطور اللعبة. فقد حالت العقوبات الدولية والقيود المصرفية التي فُرضت على سوريا دون وصول ملايين الدولارات من مخصصات التطوير التي يقدمها «فيفا» إلى الاتحاد السوري، مما حدّ من
